Edit for 1.0 release: ok so. it's dramatically better. but it's gone from feeling like pre-alpha to feeling alright. it's more fun, systems work together better, combat feels better, upgrades are more interesting, there's more silly events in the world (like volcanoes erupting) that are fun the first time you see them. but ultimately the game boils down to running around open levels shooting egg blobs and changing body parts. there's not much more to it still. TL;DR: Systems are good, game plays better, but the gameplay loop itself is bland. Drop into level, shoot eggs, get some new body parts, repeat. ----- Unfortunately I'd say wait on this. Needs more time to cook even for early access, it feels pre-alpha and like not much has changed since the playtests. The UI looks placeholder and messy, the missions are a mess and take about an hour to do a single run, 3 currencies but I'm not sure what I do with any of them, the game crashed when I closed it. They still have the 'wishlist on steam' button in the escape menu from when the build was for the playtest/demo. Will happily change my review once there's enough of a game to feel like it's early access and I'm not paying for the privilege to test a pre-alpha build.

SWAPMEAT is a refreshing take on the cooperative roguelite shooter genre, developed and published by One More Game. Instead of relying on conventional character progression systems, the game introduces a bizarre and entertaining mechanic that allows players to harvest body parts from defeated alien creatures and attach them to their own character. This unusual concept forms the foundation of the entire experience, giving SWAPMEAT a distinctive identity that immediately separates it from the countless roguelites currently available on the market. While the premise may sound absurd at first, the developers successfully transform it into a surprisingly deep gameplay system that rewards experimentation and creativity. Players assume the role of a corporate operative exploring dangerous alien worlds on behalf of a futuristic company. Every mission sends them into hostile environments packed with strange creatures, each possessing unique abilities that can be stolen and repurposed. Heads, torsos, and legs can all be swapped individually, creating an enormous number of possible combinations. Rather than collecting simple stat upgrades, players continuously modify their character's anatomy, unlocking entirely new combat skills and movement options. This mechanic encourages constant adaptation because the effectiveness of a build depends on how well different body parts work together. Combat is one of the game's strongest elements. Battles are fast-paced, energetic, and often chaotic as waves of enemies flood the screen from multiple directions. The shooting mechanics feel responsive, but what truly elevates the action is the ability system attached to harvested body parts. One combination may favor aggressive close-range attacks, while another focuses on mobility, crowd control, or defensive support. Since players can alter their setup throughout a run, combat remains dynamic and rarely falls into repetitive patterns. The result is a gameplay loop that consistently rewards experimentation rather than encouraging players to rely on a single optimal strategy. The roguelite structure is well integrated into the overall design. Every expedition presents randomized encounters, different enemy types, and unpredictable opportunities to collect new biological upgrades. Because no two runs provide the exact same resources, players are forced to improvise and discover synergies they may never have considered before. This unpredictability keeps the experience engaging over long play sessions and significantly enhances replay value. Even failed runs feel worthwhile because they often reveal new combinations or strategies that can be applied in future attempts. Cooperative play serves as the heart of the experience. Although the game can be enjoyed solo, it clearly shines when played with friends. Teams of up to four players can tackle missions together, creating entertaining situations where each player develops wildly different mutations and combat roles. The cooperative structure encourages communication and coordination without becoming overly demanding. Dynamic scaling also helps maintain challenge regardless of team size, ensuring that both solo and multiplayer sessions remain enjoyable. Watching teammates assemble ridiculous alien body combinations adds a layer of humor that complements the game's overall tone. Visually, SWAPMEAT embraces a colorful and exaggerated science-fiction aesthetic. The alien creatures are imaginative and often grotesque in amusing ways, while the environments feature a wide variety of strange locations filled with personality. The art direction prioritizes creativity over realism, which fits perfectly with the game's absurd premise. Animations effectively communicate the impact of combat and the transformations caused by body swapping, helping every new mutation feel meaningful. The presentation consistently reinforces the game's playful identity. Another noteworthy aspect is the progression system outside of individual runs. Resources earned during missions can be invested in permanent upgrades, additional equipment, and other long-term improvements. This structure creates a satisfying sense of advancement without undermining the importance of skill and experimentation. Players gradually unlock more possibilities while still needing to make smart decisions during each run. The balance between permanent progression and randomized gameplay ensures that the game remains rewarding over extended periods. The humor deserves recognition as well. SWAPMEAT never attempts to be a serious science-fiction adventure. Instead, it embraces its ridiculous concept wholeheartedly, filling the experience with quirky corporate satire, strange creatures, and outrageous body-part combinations. The comedic tone helps maintain a lighthearted atmosphere even during intense battles, making the game approachable and memorable. Fortunately, the humor rarely overshadows the gameplay and instead serves as an effective complement to the action. The game is not entirely free of shortcomings. New players may initially find the large number of body-part combinations overwhelming, and some builds naturally feel stronger or more exciting than others. The heavy emphasis on randomness can occasionally lead to less satisfying runs depending on available upgrades. Additionally, players looking for a deep narrative experience may find the story secondary to the gameplay systems. However, these issues do little to diminish the overall quality of the experience. SWAPMEAT succeeds because it commits fully to its central idea and builds every aspect of the game around it. The body-swapping mechanic is not merely a novelty but a genuinely engaging system that influences combat, progression, cooperation, and replayability. Combined with entertaining multiplayer action, imaginative world design, and strong roguelite foundations, the game delivers a unique experience that feels fresh within a crowded genre. For fans of cooperative shooters and roguelites looking for something unconventional, SWAPMEAT offers a creative and highly enjoyable adventure. Rating: 8/10

一开始以为又是那种同质化严重打击感稀碎的路边小肉鸽，但实际体验下来东西游戏可玩性还不错。 说说这游戏战斗方面的系统。 重头戏的是有能给玩家属性加成和独特技能的尸块系统，搭配不同的尸块达成玩家清怪和机动的需求是一个还不错的策略玩点。 击杀小怪完成任务获得经验，获得属性升级和武器的元素质变，以及会根据你武器元素给你最多6个机制方面的升级，这些升级能让你单元素成体系多元素也能combo，这方面做得差强人意。 这游戏在局内的战斗走的是黑夜君临鸦卫奇旅那种路子，有限的发育时间鼓励玩家提高输出和采取激进的打法来提高发育效率，同时在一定程度上考验玩家的时间管理，这算是我比较喜欢的玩点。 这游戏设定一开始看上去猎奇但算有趣和有想象力，再加上一些黑色幽默还挺有意思的。 在内容方面我还没体验多少，但2小时打下来这游戏还算能让我保持新鲜感，是有一定的内容量的。 这游戏目前的缺点就是中文汉化做得不是很好，枪械打击感很烂，换弹癌容易按r键老是把主动丢出去，字体挡视野也很难看，但这些我看小作坊制作组是很难完善好的。 但整体来说我觉得是不错的，这游戏还能喝朋友一起玩，属于是值得一试的80分作品！

[b]I'm leaving this review a little early just because I'm worried there might not be enough eyes on this game.[/b] Swapmeat is going to remind you of several games at first glance, but once you get into a meat of it, it becomes clear this is something incredibly unique. The art and animations are truly a marvel to behold. Everything is at odds with itself, gross and squelchy, superbly silly, dark and dire, it goes through so many tonal shifts that you're just left in awe not really knowing what will come next. The quality of everything is also through the roof. Harder enemies have completely unique skins, every part has unique animations for every sort of bodily action, I don't know how they can charge this little for the amount of work that was done... Gameplay-wise, the game just FEELS good to play. For a game where your own body is constantly shifting and changing shape, the game does a fantastic job at just making it feel right to move around the world with guns blazing and shots firing out of brand new orifices. The game uses tried and true systems that most roguelites use but always seems to put a unique spin on everything it implements. The objective gameplay is a bit difficult to grasp but after failing a few times you'll start to get an idea of what you need to do. Audio is something I also have to point out separately. It has a truly horrid and perfect amount of squelching and screaming and moaning. The music is something I'd expect anywhere from blasting at a backyard cookout to some obscure Japanese fishing game on the PS2, and every track is extremely fun to listen to, especially the vocal(!?) tracks in the lobby. (There's some issues with volume in the current patch but the devs seem to be constantly fixing things past the 1.0 release so hopefully this will be fixed by the time you read this) [b]Overall, this is a silly, squelchy, fun and frantic game made by people who clearly had a ton of fun making it. For the asking price you'll definitely be getting your moneys worth especially with a few friends to share a good laugh with, so get out there and swap your meat!![/b]

This feels more fun to play than RoR 2, but this in no way is a 1.0 release. It's an Early Access game with Early Access game issues. The sound is awful, is too loud and cacophonous with the default settings (and it can still somehow stay loud at 10% volume, with some sounds becoming way too quiet, and some bursting your eardrums). And yet you are supposed to use sound to identify and deal with specific threats. The performance is unstable. There is nothing in this game that should be tanking a modern 3090-based rig to below 60, let alone below 30 FPS, and yet it does, at least a few times per level. The balance is weird. The maps are pretty huge while your basic movement speed is pretty slow. You are on a timer though, so if you aren't moving quickly, you aren't doing much in time. But there are so many cool 'meats' that don't add mobility, and it just feels sub-optimal to be using them. The progression is unnecessarily grindy. I get that it's supposed to keep me hooked and extend the replay-ability, but it just starts feeling like an annoying chore way too soon. Bosses are just boring damage sponges. They could have had two times less health and nothing of value would have been lost. I would personally like an 'auto-fire' option in the settings. With how many enemies the game is throwing at you (especially in co-op), there are very few moments when I don't want to be firing my gun, since the ammo is unlimited and the reload mini-game is actually pretty fun to do (and buffs your damage if you got the right upgrades). Holding the left mouse button down for long periods of time is uncomfortable and painful, so I don't see why this couldn't be an option. All in all, a bit too pricey for what is essentially a mislabeled early access playtest.
